transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-08-05
Time: 16:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jesse Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (Mariner Eng), Priya Shah (Mariner Platform), Liam O'Connor (Mariner Security)

Auto-generated summary: Quickstart + sandbox provisioning and API walkthrough; action items to share docs and schedule POC.

[00:00] Jesse: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm jesse from redwood, and with me is maya our solutions engineer. how's the audio?
[00:10] Daniel: good here, thanks. we got about an hour, excited to see the quickstart flow.
[00:15] Maya: awesome, we'll run through sandbox provisioning first, then auth and a live python + ts snippet, and finish with the console and some optimize tips. feel free to interrupt.
[00:22] Jesse: small note — we'll show hosted sandbox keys; if you want a private vpc later that's fine but for the poc hosted sandbox is fastest.
[00:30] Priya: yeah timeline wise we want to validate within two weeks, and evaluate cost/latency. also security will need a KMS/rotation story.
[00:40] Liam: and SOC2 artifacts, right, plus audit logs.
[00:44] Maya: absolutely, we'll share our security pack. okay starting sandbox provisioning — step one is create an org in the console, step two is generate an API key under settings, set it as a read/write token or restricted; for dev we usually scope to inference only.
[01:10] Jesse: i'll paste the link in chat to the quickstart doc after. sometimes the console screenshots show "Redwood Console" but the transcription might show redwood conch or something — ignore that.
[01:20] Daniel: haha noted. on the API key, can we rotate keys programmatically? we have an automated secret rotation workflow.
[01:26] Maya: yes, keys can be rotated via the API and we support short-lived tokens through our integration with KMS/H-S-M — users often call it K M S or HSM, sometimes spelled out. for the hosted sandbox we provide a temp key you can rotate.
[01:42] Daniel: great. what's the recommended env var name for CI? we use GITHUB_ACTIONS and vault.
[01:48] Maya: common pattern is REDWOOD_API_KEY or REDWOOD_TOKEN. store in your secret manager, never check into repo. our sample repo uses process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY for node and os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY') for python.
[02:10] [small crosstalk — someone typing]
[02:20] Maya: i'm gonna switch to a live demo — showing the python quickstart. first pip install redwood-sdk or similar. note: package name in the doc is redwood-inference-python (might show slightly different)
[02:36] [05:05] Maya: code snippet, from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')); resp = client.generate("Summarize this shipment note...") — the generate call returns a streaming generator or full payload depending on your call.
[05:20] Daniel: streaming support is important for us — we do progressive UI updates. any latency numbers for streaming vs non?
[05:26] Maya: streaming has slight warmup but gives perceived latency improvements. for our hosted sandbox typical p50 single-token latency on small models is ~30-60ms; but depends on model, seq length, and hardware. we'll attach perf profiles in the doc.
[06:00] Priya: do we need special headers for function calling? we plan to use tool calling patterns.
[06:06] Maya: function/tool-calling is supported — you provide a function schema in the call, and results come back with a tool response. header-wise it's standard JSON body, no extra special header beyond auth.
[06:20] [06:50] Jesse: switching to TypeScript quickstart — node package is @redwood/inference or similar in the example. snippet: import { Redwood } from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood(process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY); const out = await client.chat.create(...).
[07:15] Daniel: do you have a minimal TS example for embeddings and storing vectors?
[07:22] Maya: yes — we show embeddings.create(model='text-embed-001', input='...') and the response includes vector floats. note: SDK also has built-in batch helpers for embeddings to reduce requests.
[07:40] Daniel: batching — is that client-side or server-side? we have burst traffic patterns.
[07:46] Maya: both. client SDK includes simple batching helper; at the platform layer we do continuous batching and auto-batch where it makes sense. you can tune batching in the console per route. the Optimize tab will recommend batch sizes based on sequence length distribution. sometimes the transcript shows K-V cash instead of K-V cache — yes we have KV cache for chat state.
[08:20] Priya: regarding costs — do you expose per-token cost in the console so we can map to our invoices?
[08:27] Jesse: yep, Console shows token-level cost breakdowns, per-model and per-route costs. we'll share some sample billing exports for the POC.
[08:40] Liam: for security — how does the private deployment differ? we may need on-prem later.
[08:46] Maya: private deployment gives you a private control plane, option for VPC or on-prem package, and you manage KMS. hosted has encryption at rest managed by redwood; private you bring your own KMS/HSM. we have audit logs in both but retention differs by plan.
[09:10] Liam: do you support SSO/SAML for the console?
[09:14] Jesse: yes, SSO via SAML and SCIM for provisioning. we'll include setup docs.
[09:20] [10:00] Maya: i'll run a quick live run — calling the api from python:
>>> import os
>>> from redwood import Client
>>> c = Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
>>> r = c.generate("Create a delivery summary: pickup at port X...")
[10:25] Maya: we see the response — little typos in transcript, sometimes "deliver" becomes "deliverer" — but the payload is JSON with tokens, choices, and metadata including model_id and cost estimate.
[10:40] Daniel: what's the best practice for prompt versioning? we want to maintain reproducibility.
[10:46] Maya: store prompts as templated assets in your repo; our console also supports pinning model versions and you can tie a prompt set to a rollout. Optimize can snapshot prompts for regression testing.
[11:05] Jesse: quick detour — if you want to test latency across regions we can provision endpoints in us-west, eu-west, etc. For POC we'll usually put it in the nearest region.
[11:20] Priya: that'd be good. our infra is in us-east and europe.
[11:25] Maya: okay switching to CI/CICD notes — in CI use ephemeral sandbox keys injected as env vars and lock scopes to inference-only. for e2e tests spin up the small bench harness we provide.
[12:10] [12:45] Daniel: about quotas — can you set per-key quotas so our dev teams don't blow budget?
[12:50] Jesse: yes, console supports per-key rate limits and quotas; also usage alerts.
[13:10] Maya: now Optimize recommendations — it will suggest batching thresholds, when to cache prefixes in the KV cache, and whether a quantized model variant is acceptable based on your quality thresholds. we'll show an example rule: for chat routes with median query length < 128 tokens use q4_0 quantized model to save ~40% cost.
[13:40] Daniel: any regressions when quantizing? we worry about hallucinations.
[13:46] Maya: that's why Optimize ties to evals: you can run prompt evals against both baseline and quantized models; if quality drops beyond threshold Optimize will alert.
[14:10] [14:55] Priya: send the eval harness please.
[15:00] Jesse: will do.
[15:10] [15:40] Maya: switching to demoing console — i'm sharing screen, top-left is routes, middle is models, right is metrics. you can pin a model version per route, set rollout %, and configure fallback to a cheaper model.
[16:00] Daniel: fallback is interesting — if a high-cost model saturates it falls back to cached or cheaper variant?
[16:06] Maya: correct — policy can say: try model-A; if latency > 500ms or queue depth > N fallback to model-B. we also support region fallback.
[16:30] [17:00] Jesse: quick nit: when you see "model-B" in docs that's sometimes redwood-sim-2 in examples — please ignore toy names.
[17:12] Liam: audit logs — can you export to our SIEM?
[17:16] Maya: yes, we have syslog and S3 export options and also API access to raw audit events. for private deployments you can forward logs internally.
[17:40] Daniel: for embeddings storage, do you provide a managed vector DB?
[17:46] Maya: we don't provide a full managed vector DB in hosted by default, but we have connectors and reference code to push embeddings into common stores (e.g. Pinecone, Milvus, or your Postgres with pgvector). we can include an example pipeline.
[18:10] [18:40] Priya: dependency/versioning — what's the SDK stability? semver?
[18:45] Maya: yes semver, major bumps for breaking changes and we provide migration guides. we also publish a changelog in the console.
[19:05] Daniel: any readiness for air-gapped setups?
[19:10] Maya: private on-prem package supports air-gapped installs; there's an installation checklist including container image transfer and offline activation. that's higher-effort and often a later phase after POC.
[19:35] [20:00] Maya: quick live test — i'll run an embeddings batch call using the batching helper to show reduced request count.
[20:25] [20:40] Maya: output shows 10 inputs batched into 2 requests, and server-side metric shows fewer tokens billed because we cache repeated prefixes.
[21:05] Daniel: nice. about token accounting — is the cached prefix counted each time?
[21:10] Maya: cached prefix is not re-sent, but billing model shows requests and tokens after cache savings. we'll send detailed billing export sample.
[21:30] [22:00] Priya: okay on POC success criteria — for us it's: 1) latency p95 < 400ms for the main route in eu-west, 2) cost per 1k tokens below threshold X, 3) no data exfiltration concerns with hosted sandbox.
[22:25] Jesse: good, we'll put those in the POC doc.
[22:40] Liam: one more on encryption keys — for hosted you manage rotation via our KMS integration, does that mean keys are in our KMS or redwood's?
[22:50] Maya: for hosted we can integrate with your cloud KMS (e.g., GCP KMS or AWS KMS) via cross-account role so you keep control. for private you fully manage keys.
[23:10] [24:00] Daniel: any hard limits on sequence length? our docs say up to 2048 tokens, is that right?
[24:06] Maya: depends on model; many open models vary. we'll include model-specific profiles — some support 4096+ but perf differs.
[24:30] Jesse: quickly back to SDK — here's a sample CI step for GitHub Actions to run a quick generate and assert response schema. Put the API key in GH secrets as REDWOOD_API_KEY.
[25:00] [26:10] Maya: note: if transcription turns product names odd (e.g., "Optimize" as "optimizee") our docs are canonical.
[26:30] Daniel: are there rate-limit headers in responses? we want to surface remaining quota in our app.
[26:35] Maya: yes responses include X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining equivalents, and the SDK surfaces them in a metadata object.
[27:00] Priya: about retention of training data — do you retain customer prompts for product improvements?
[27:06] Jesse: by default we do not use customer data to train models; there's a data usage policy and options to opt out. private deployments keep data in-customer environment. we'll attach the policy doc.
[27:30] [28:00] Daniel: ok, can you show the console's optimize recommendation for a specific route?
[28:10] Maya: sure — example: route "delivery-summary" shows median len 96, suggested batch size 8, recommended quantized candidate q4_0 with rollback in case of eval drop.
[28:40] [29:10] Jesse: time check — 30 minutes gone, we've got about 28 left. any deep dive requests?
[29:20] Daniel: maybe a quick network topology for VPC?
[29:25] Maya: high level: private control plane connects to customer VPC via an endpoint, model runtime nodes can be in that VPC and we support security groups, firewalls, and private endpoints. diagram in our private deployment playbook.
[30:00] [31:10] Liam: one more — key rotation with HSM — can you do automatic rotation or only manual?
[31:18] Maya: both. if you integrate an external KMS you can configure rotation policies and we will pick up rotated keys; for hosted we also offer managed rotation schedules.
[31:50] [33:00] Maya: quick note on debugging — console has a trace view per request so you can see token timings, kernel selection, and whether it used KV cache or batching. helps debug spikes. sometimes transcript shows "kernel" as "carol" but it's kernel.
[33:40] Daniel: excellent.
[33:50] Maya: final live demo — run a small bench harness we include: send 100 requests to a route with concurrency 8. shows throughput and error rates.
[34:20] [35:00] Maya: results show p50 120ms p95 430ms in us-west region for that test. if you need colder numbers we'll run your payloads in the POC.
[35:35] Daniel: would be great to run our payloads.
[35:40] Jesse: for POC we'll ask for a small corpus and a few prompt templates.
[35:50] Priya: timeline — we aim to start POC next week.
[36:00] [37:10] Jesse: next steps recap: jesse will send sandbox guide + creds; maya will share quickstart repo and bench harness; customer confirms POC success criteria and stakeholders.
[37:30] Priya: sounds good.
[37:40] Liam: i'll compile the list of compliance questions and send to jesse.
[37:50] Jesse: awesome. any other questions?
[38:00] [38:30] Daniel: minor — do you have an example of a fallback policy JSON for the console?
[38:36] Maya: yes, will include a sample fallback policy and an example of a canary rollout config.
[39:00] [41:00] [lots of small clarifications and intermittent cross talk, a few times audio glitches caused a speaker to repeat]
[42:10] Maya: one more tip — prefer shorter initial context to reduce cost; Optimize will surface where you can trim.
[42:40] Daniel: ok.
[43:00] Jesse: closing notes — we'll also attach security pack and SOC2 snapshot.
[43:20] Priya: thank you, appreciate the thorough walkthrough.
[43:30] Daniel: thanks all.
[43:40] Jesse: we'll follow up with docs and schedule that POC kickoff for 2025-08-12 unless you prefer a different date.
[43:55] Priya: 8/12 works.
[44:05] Jesse: perfect, thanks everyone — talk soon.

End of transcript.

References shared in chat: https://redwood.example.com/docs/sdk-quickstart; https://redwood.example.com/docs/sandbox-provisioning; Security pack (link emailed)
